body:
I don't use python very often, but when I do, I use black. Coming from a rust background, the more "controversial" features seem like the sensible thing to me. Vertical code is (IMO) usually easier to reason about than horizontal code, and python can get very horizontal.

I'm less sure about `standardize_type_comments` - changing comments seems strange to me. But, if there are other rules that alter comments, there is a reasonable precedent for this.

Agree that everything `fix_type_expansion_split` and below should be stabilised!

I ran `black --preview` on a sizable fraction of a giant codebase.

- `multiline_string_handling` looks great, we should stabilise it
- `wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens` results in a tonne of change. A lot of it actually isn't great, I kind of don't want it. A lot of putting a really long string on its own line, which just eats more vertical space, and makes the dict keys harder to scan.
- `wrap_comprehension_in ` is mostly great, but in a few cases removes parentheses that makes things harder to read. I opened https://github.com/psf/black/issues/4877 , ideally we would fix this

I didn't test `remove_parens_from_assignment_lhs` because I was using 25.11

> * `wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens` results in a tonne of change. A lot of it actually isn't great, I kind of don't want it. A lot of putting a really long string on its own line, which just eats more vertical space, and makes the dict keys harder to scan.

@hauntsaninja Are you able to share examples?

Related: #4158 which asked for the opposite (more wrapping) and was implemented last year

This feature has been around for over 2 years so we should probably try to reach a decision on it soon

issue.title: Thinking about `wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens`
issue.body:
In https://github.com/psf/black/issues/4875#issuecomment-3593650163 while testing, I kind of felt like I didn't want `wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens`.

I get why `wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens` could make sense, and this feeling I'm feeling isn't the most principled feeling, which is why I didn't make an issue earlier — open and curious to other people's thoughts. I think part of what I'm reacting to is seeing this in the aggregate, e.g. this would add literally tens of thousands of lines to the codebase I'm testing on.

body: Good spot on #4158. I don't know that this is my most principled opinion, but posted some examples in https://github.com/psf/black/issues/4882 . Curious what folks' takes here are, or if other people have opinions on `wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens` from trying it out on their codebases!

> An unobjective change, but can cause lots of churn, and was added very recently (Not released yet, will hopefully be in a 25.12).

Ideally every change we make should be in the preview style at least once, so would be good to get this in a 25.12. I get the impression that this particular change won't touch a lot of code, so probably not a big deal.

I tried `black --preview` on a couple of open-source codebases (my work codebase is much bigger but Shantanu already covered it). Mostly I see few changes and I like the changes that I see; most seem to be from multiline_string_handling.

In mypy I'm not sure we should be removing these parens:

```diff
diff --git a/mypy/graph_utils.py b/mypy/graph_utils.py
index 154efcef4..a58c58bf9 100644
--- a/mypy/graph_utils.py
+++ b/mypy/graph_utils.py
@@ -113,5 +113,5 @@ def topsort(data: dict[T, set[T]]) -> Iterable[set[T]]:
         if not ready:
             break
         yield ready
-        data = {item: (dep - ready) for item, dep in data.items() if item not in ready}
+        data = {item: dep - ready for item, dep in data.items() if item not in ready}
     assert not data, f"A cyclic dependency exists amongst {data!r}"
```

This is another example of `wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens`. I think I'm fine with the reformatting here but there may be cases where it's worse.

Also a case where removing parens from a comprehension is clearly a positive change:

```diff
diff --git a/mypy/test/helpers.py b/mypy/test/helpers.py
index d5f1cd787..7e7db1b32 100644
--- a/mypy/test/helpers.py
+++ b/mypy/test/helpers.py
@@ -481,7 +481,7 @@ def normalize_report_meta(content: list[str]) -> list[str]:
 def find_test_files(pattern: str, exclude: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
     return [
         path.name
-        for path in (pathlib.Path(test_data_prefix).rglob(pattern))
+        for path in pathlib.Path(test_data_prefix).rglob(pattern)
         if path.name not in (exclude or [])
     ]
 
```

So overall I'm positive on these changes, though we should consider tweaking or deferring the parens-related ones.
The changes for Pillow with Black 26.1a1 look good to me 👍 https://github.com/hugovk/Pillow/commit/485ed4ec3a629ceccdfe13479c6349e13a3bdc28

Just tested the preview style for pylint (with `25.12.0`).

**`wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens`**
Not entirely sure about this one, especially for strings. There are some good examples, e.g.
```diff
             {
                 "type": "csv",
                 "metavar": "<modules>",
                 "default": (),
-                "help": "List of plugins (as comma separated values of "
-                "python module names) to load, usually to register "
-                "additional checkers.",
+                "help": (
+                    "List of plugins (as comma separated values of "
+                    "python module names) to load, usually to register "
+                    "additional checkers."
+                ),
             },
```

However for single line ones it's arguably worse. Especially if it's just a few chars over the line length limit. I'd definitely add `# fmt: off` in a few places because of it.
```diff
             {
                 "default": False,
                 "type": "yn",
                 "metavar": "<y or n>",
-                "help": "Include a hint for the correct naming format with invalid-name.",
+                "help": (
+                    "Include a hint for the correct naming format with invalid-name."
+                ),
             },
```

**`multiline_string_handling`**
I like it. Yes it causes a bit of churn but it always looked kind of strange to have this on separate lines.
```py
"""
)
```

**`wrap_comprehension_in`**
We do have a similar example to #4877 where the parentheses were added for additional clarity, removing them feels wrong.
```diff
-       kwargs = {keyword.arg for keyword in (node.keywords or ())}
+       kwargs = {keyword.arg for keyword in node.keywords or ()}
```

For multiline examples, yes it is consistent but I always felt like wrapping something without any operators just so the line length is kept below the limit, isn't great.
```diff
                 any(
                     other_node_final_statement is closest_try_finally_ancestor
                     or other_node_final_statement.parent_of(
                         closest_try_finally_ancestor
                     )
-                    for other_node_final_statement in other_node_try_finally_ancestor.finalbody
+                    for other_node_final_statement in (
+                        other_node_try_finally_ancestor.finalbody
+                    )
                 )
```
_If it were up to me, I'd also prefer `closest_try_finally_ancestor` to be on the same line with `other_node_final_statement.parent_of` (though not related to this particular change)._

Thanks for the feedback! FWIW @cdce8p, we're expecting to defer `wrap_long_dict_values_in_parens` and `wrap_comprehension_in` to next year (hence they're not included in 26.1a1). The insights are still appreciated though!

body:
My gut reaction is that I don't like `remove_parens_from_assignment_lhs`. I use assignment unpacking sparingly, and I prefer it to be visually different from standard assignment, so I can easily pick it out. Assignment unpacking is typically a code smell and I like to be reminded when code is using it so I can keep potential refactorings in mind.

Compare:

```diff
         # split constants into two pools, so we still have a good chance to draw
         # global constants even if there are many local constants.
-        (global_constants, local_constants) = CONSTANTS_CACHE[key]
+        global_constants, local_constants = CONSTANTS_CACHE[key]
         constants_lists = ([global_constants] if global_constants else []) + (
             [local_constants] if local_constants else []
         )
         if not constants_lists:
             return None
```

(I recognize that giving feedback after the stable style has been set is rather pointless, and that black sets a preview window for exactly this reason. I don't always remember to opt in each year, but that's on me, not black 🙂. Thanks as always for maintaining black.)

Re `multiline_string_handling` in general I like having my open and close parentheses at the same indentation level, so like:

```py
print(
    conn.sql(
        """
        SQL code line 1
        SQL code line 2
        """
    )
)
```

(Note the indented trailing `"""` -- I mainly work with SQL code where trailing whitespace doesn't matter)

IMO it makes it a bit easier to skim through and tell when something starts or ends. Now `black` wants it to dangle which looks a bit different compared to the rest of my code with non-dangling blocks like

```py
Foo.bar(
    key1=value1,
    key2=value2,
)
```

Maybe I'll just eventually get used to the new look though, given that it's already been stabilised.

@abeliangroupie I agree that in this case the new formatting isn't automatically ideal. In this case, I'd recommend manually reformatting it to:
```py
print(conn.sql("""
    SQL code line 1
    SQL code line 2
"""))
```
Black wouldn't make that change on its own because it changes string contents.

issue.title: feat(triggers): replace anywhere-detection with direct-only scripture triggers
issue.body:
<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Overview

This PR introduces a trigger mode system that replaces the flexible, configurable scripture reference detection with a strict "direct-only" mode. The bot now responds only when the entire incoming message is a scripture reference, eliminating support for embedded references and the `detect_references_anywhere` configuration option. This refactoring centralizes trigger detection into a dedicated module and moves book normalization utilities into a validation module.

## Key Changes

**Features**
- Add new `triggers.py` module with `TriggerSource` enum (`DIRECT`) and `TriggerMatch` dataclass containing `passage`, `translation`, and `source` fields
- Add `detect_trigger(body, default_translation)` function that returns a `TriggerMatch` only for whole-message scripture references
- Add `TRIGGER_MODE_DIRECT_ONLY` constant to `constants/bible.py`
- Add `validation.py` module exporting `validate_and_normalize_book_name()` function for canonical book name normalization

**Refactors**
- Refactor `BibleBot.on_room_message()` to delegate reference detection to `detect_trigger()` instead of inline pattern matching
- Move book name normalization logic from `bot.py` to new `validation.py` module
- Remove `PARTIAL_REFERENCE_PATTERNS` from `constants/bible.py` (full-match only)
- Remove inline reference detection pattern logic from `bot.py` (~89 lines removed)
- Update imports across test files to use functions from their new module locations

**Removals**
- Remove `detect_references_anywhere` configuration option from `constants/config.py` and all documentation
- Remove support for detecting scripture references embedded in longer text
- Remove support for partial/anywhere reference matching in Matrix bridge scenarios

**Tests**
- Add comprehensive `test_trigger_policy.py` with 171 lines of tests for direct-only trigger detection and bot integration
- Simplify reference detection tests in `test_bot.py` by removing parametrized `detect_references_anywhere` toggle tests
- Update integration tests (`test_integration_patterns.py`) to validate direct-only behavior with new test cases for embedded and longer sentence scenarios
- Update all test imports to use `validate_and_normalize_book_name` from `validation.py`
- Update mocked event objects to set `event.formatted_body = None` in reference-detection tests

**Documentation**
- Update README to require sending scripture references as standalone messages
- Replace "Flexible References" feature bullet with "Direct-Only Triggers"
- Add "Reference Detection" section documenting trigger behavior with explicit examples of what triggers and what doesn't
- Update `CONFIGURATION.md` to document direct-only semantics and remove `detect_references_anywhere` configuration reference
- Remove `detect_references_anywhere` commented options from `sample_config.yaml`

**Infrastructure**
- Add `.trunk/trunk` bash launcher script for bootstrapping Trunk CLI binaries
- Update `.trunk/trunk.yaml` with newer linter versions (bandit, black, checkov, isort, markdownlint, prettier, ruff, yamllint) and add renovate
- Add `.codex` to `.gitignore`

## Breaking Changes

The `detect_references_anywhere` configuration option has been removed. Any configurations using this setting should be updated:
- Remove `detect_references_anywhere: true` or `detect_references_anywhere: false` from config files
- The bot now operates in "direct-only" mode exclusively
- Scripture references embedded within natural language text will no longer trigger a response (e.g., "I like John 3:16" will not trigger)
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
